common_name: Sieboldiana Clematis (Passion Flower Double White-and-Purple Clematis)

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered, mild spot with roots shaded and cool; this variety prefers gentle climates and dislikes extreme heat or hard winters.

directions: Train this old Japanese cultivar up a trellis or through an open shrub where its oddly beautiful flowers can be admired at close range: creamy-white sepals surround a dense, frilly rosette of purple petal-like staminodes, giving each bloom a distinctly double, bicolor look. It flowers over a long stretch from early summer into fall and performs best in a sheltered site with mild winters and summers, since it is less tolerant of temperature extremes than many large-flowered hybrids. Keep the root zone cool and shaded with mulch or low companion plants while the vine itself reaches for full sun. Light pruning to remove dead growth after the coldest part of winter is usually all it needs.

common_name: Rehderiana Clematis (Nodding Fragrant Primrose-Bell Species Clematis)

planting.note: Give this vigorous species plenty of room, or cut it back hard each spring to keep it to a more manageable size on a smaller support.

directions: This vigorous Chinese species climbs rapidly over a fence, arbor, or large shrub, where its loose clusters of small, nodding, bell-shaped flowers open pale primrose-yellow and fade to a soft parchment tone as they age. The real draw is fragrance: the blooms carry a distinctive sweet, cowslip-like scent that drifts well beyond the plant from midsummer into autumn. It prefers its top growth in full sun while the roots stay cool and shaded, and because it flowers on the current season's growth, an annual hard pruning in late winter keeps the vine full and floriferous rather than bare at the base. Give it generous space or a sturdy large structure, since left unchecked it can climb considerably higher than most garden clematis.

common_name: Lady Bird Johnson Clematis (Fuchsia-Red Nodding Texas Clematis)

planting.note: Pruning group three; blooms on new growth, so cut the vine back hard to about a foot above the ground each late winter.

directions: Like other hybrids descended from the Texas native leatherflower, this cultivar produces small, thick-textured, nodding bells in rich fuchsia-red that dangle from wiry stems rather than facing outward, opening steadily from summer into early fall. Grow it up a narrow obelisk or wire trellis, or let it thread through a sturdy shrub, keeping the root zone cool and shaded beneath mulch while the vine itself climbs into full sun. It shares its Texas parent's tolerance for heat and dry spells, making it a sound choice for warmer gardens where large-flowered hybrids struggle. Because flowers form only on new wood, prune the whole vine back hard each late winter to encourage a full new flush of growth.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown a couple of inches below the soil surface; this is one of the hardiest and earliest clematis to bloom.

directions: Among the hardiest clematis available, this alpine selection bears nodding, bell-shaped flowers with long, pointed, deep purple-blue sepals and a cluster of purple stamens, opening in April and May ahead of nearly every other clematis in the garden. Silky, feathery seed heads follow the flowers and remain decorative on the vine well into summer. It tolerates cold, exposed sites that would damage less hardy types, making it a good choice for northern gardens or windswept spots. Because it flowers entirely on the previous year's growth, prune only lightly right after blooming to remove dead wood and shape the plant.

common_name: Early Sensation Clematis (Evergreen Fragrant White Winter-Spring Clematis)

planting.note: Site against a sheltered, sunny wall or fence; this evergreen hybrid is less cold-hardy than deciduous clematis and appreciates winter protection in colder parts of its range.

directions: This evergreen hybrid clothes its support year-round in finely divided foliage that emerges bronze and matures to glossy dark green, then opens scented, white, bell-to-cup-shaped flowers with a soft greenish-yellow center from late winter into early spring, well before most other clematis stir. It is a female selection, so when grown near a compatible male plant it can set attractive fluffy seed heads after bloom. Grow it against a warm, sheltered wall or fence in full sun with good drainage, since it is noticeably less cold-hardy than deciduous alpine or montana types. Prune lightly right after flowering to control size and remove any winter-damaged growth.

common_name: Blue Bird Clematis (Nodding Lavender-Blue Macropetala Clematis)

planting.note: Exceptionally cold-hardy and one of the earliest clematis to bloom in northern gardens; needs no regular pruning beyond light shaping after flowering.

directions: Bred for cold-winter climates, this macropetala selection produces small, semi-double, nodding, lavender-blue bells with contrasting white-and-yellow stamens, blooming heavily in spring with occasional light repeat flowering in late summer. After the main bloom, smoky, silvery seed heads form and persist on the vine, adding a second season of interest. It is extremely cold-tolerant and among the earliest clematis to open in northern gardens, making it a good companion for spring bulbs on a fence or low trellis. Since it flowers on the previous year's wood, prune only lightly right after blooming to tidy the plant.

common_name: Little Rootie Tootie Daylily (Miniature Cherry-Red Plicata Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a heavily budded compact miniature well suited to edging and containers.

directions: This compact miniature carries small, rounded, cherry-red flowers patterned with darker plicata veining above a tiny green throat edged in white, each bloom only about two and a half inches across on scapes under two feet tall. It carries an unusually heavy bud count for its size, opening in early to midseason with a capacity for some rebloom later on. Because the whole plant stays low and dense, it works well massed along a path edge, tucked into a mixed border, or grown in a container where larger daylilies would be out of scale. Divide the clumps every few years once flowering begins to taper off to keep the display dense and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give it room, since its flowers and scapes run larger than most daylilies.

directions: This dormant-foliage daylily opens brilliant red flowers with a glowing chartreuse throat, each bloom stretching to roughly ten inches across with narrow, twisting, spider-like tepals that often carry extra petal segments rather than the usual six. That combination of spider form and extra petalage makes it a distinctive, much-photographed cultivar among unusual-form daylily collectors. It blooms early in the season on sturdy scapes a bit taller than average, so give it extra spacing to let the oversized flowers display without crowding neighbors. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every few years to keep the clump vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; needs generous space, since its scapes and blooms are exceptionally large.

directions: This tetraploid daylily is grown for sheer scale: fragrant, dark red-purple flowers with a green-and-yellow throat open with heavily ruffled, twisting petal edges that curl and drape downward in the crispate-cascade form, reaching diameters that dwarf an ordinary daylily bloom. Flower stalks rise well above most companion daylilies, so place it toward the back of a bed or give it its own feature spot where the oversized blooms can be appreciated. It flowers in the early-to-midseason window with some capacity for rebloom, and its dormant foliage dies back cleanly for winter. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and divide every few years as the clump becomes crowded.

common_name: Siloam Pauline Henry Daylily (Rose-Pink Siloam Series Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, like other diploid Siloam series daylilies.

directions: One of the many Arkansas-bred Siloam series daylilies, this diploid cultivar bears a clear rose-pink self flower set above a crisp green throat, with blooms exceeding four and a half inches across and a light fragrance. It opens in midseason on a compact plant typical of the Siloam line, which is prized for its well-budded scapes and clean, saturated colors. Grow it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil alongside other Siloam cultivars for a coordinated planting of compact, heavily flowering daylilies. Divide every three to four years as clumps thicken to maintain strong bloom.
